### C-R4-01
- **Locus:** 6:10–12 unit intro; slice ~L2565–L2569
- **Quote/anchor:** “This short section marks the middle of the book according to Masoretic marginal notation… Qohelet here leaves his explicit search for meaning and in the second half of the book focuses on advice and commentary about the future… anticipates the type of advice to come by telling us that it is meaningless and ultimately unhelpful.”
- **Claim:** Longman treats 6:10–12 as the book’s midpoint (Masoretic marginal note) and a transition: Qohelet shifts from explicit search for meaning toward advice/commentary on the future, while already signaling that such advice is meaningless and unhelpful.
- **Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]], [[hebel]]

### C-R4-02
- **Locus:** 6:10 commentary; ~L2577–L2579
- **Quote/anchor:** “the first part of the verse reinforces Qohelet’s belief that nothing new ever takes place (see 1:9 and 3:15)… everything has been previously named… to name is to have knowledge and control… everything that takes place has previously been known… this is a reference to God… uselessness of argument with him when he gives them a fate that they do not like.”
- **Claim:** On 6:10 Longman reads “named” via Genesis naming theology (God/Adam): prior naming means prior knowledge/control; the “stronger” opponent is God (Targum explicit), so arguing against the fate God assigns is useless.
- **Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R4-03
- **Locus:** 6:11 commentary; ~L2581–L2585
- **Quote/anchor:** “a multiplication of words is simply a multiplication of meaninglessness… no benefit for human beings in saying a lot… preferred over… ‘things’… connection with v. 10… arguments… ‘sayings’… would thus draw a close connection with the advice to follow… Whybray notes similar teaching in Proverbs 10:8, 14, 19. In the context of… Ecclesiastes… more radical.”
- **Claim:** Longman takes *debarim* as “words” (not “things”), linking fruitless argument with God to the advice chapters ahead; multiplication of words multiplies *hebel*; rhetorical question denies *yoter*/advantage; Whybray’s Proverbs parallels are noted, but Qohelet is more radical.
- **Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[proverbs]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R4-04
- **Locus:** 6:12 commentary; ~L2587–L2593
- **Quote/anchor:** “denies that it is possible to know what is good in life… reject the possibility of knowing the absolute good over against the relative good… ‘nothing better than’ formula… short (few days…) and its meaninglessness… ‘transitory’… awkwardly redundant… he made people like a shadow… God… under the sun… Qohelet never seriously entertains the thought of an afterlife… two largest problems: death and the future’s uncertainty… responsibility… squarely on God.”
- **Claim:** On 6:12 Longman: absolute good is unknowable (relative goods via “nothing better than” remain); life’s few days + *hebel* (not mere “transitory”); God makes humans shadow-like (ephemeral); future “under the sun” only—no afterlife in Qohelet’s thought; death and unknown future are Qohelet’s two largest problems, blamed on God.
- **Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R4-05
- **Locus:** 7:1–14 unit intro; ~L2595–L2605
- **Quote/anchor:** “Most recent scholars take 7:1–14 as a separate unit… Ogden… v. 13 begins a new section… vv. 13–14 operate as a kind of conclusion… shift in literary form… proverbs… ‘better-than’ pattern… Whybray… ‘attempts to see a logical progression… are probably wasted’… relative values… Some… commonplace… others intend to shock… (vv. 1b, 2, 3, 11)… Two themes… death… and wisdom and folly… inclusio… good (tob) and day (yom).”
- **Claim:** Longman delimits 7:1–14 (contra Ogden’s 13–end split): better-than proverbs (1–12) + instruction conclusion (13–14); no strict logical progression (Whybray); relative (not absolute) goods answering 6:12; mix of conventional and shocking sayings; unifying themes death and wisdom/folly; *tob*/*yom* inclusio; future unknowability returns at 7:14 (Murphy).
- **Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[proverbs]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R4-06
- **Locus:** 7:1; ~L2639–L2657
- **Quote/anchor:** “sounds as if… transposed directly from… Proverbs… good reputation… more important than fine oil… Proverbs 22:1… While the first proverb… is traditional, the second is not… death is better than birth… world-weariness… relief that life is finally over… escape from life’s oppression and meaninglessness.”
- **Claim:** 7:1a is traditional wisdom (good name > fine oil; cf. Prov 22:1, with *sem*/*semen* wordplay); 7:1b is non-traditional preference of death over birth, read as Qohelet’s world-weariness and relief that death ends oppression/*hebel*—not secured reputation (contra Targum-style readings).

### C-R4-07
- **Locus:** 7:2–4; ~L2659–L2679
- **Quote/anchor:** “better to go to a funeral than a party… live… in the recognition of their own mortality… Wright… Talmud struggled to reconcile… carpe diem… unnecessary type of theological approach… anger is better than laughter… accords with reality… Luther… sorrow rather than anger… no philological justification… Qohelet… contradicts himself at times… wise contemplate their ultimate death, while fools… live as if there is no end… tension… carpe diem… mark of a fool… confused wise man.”
- **Claim:** Funeral > feast (mortality awareness); Longman rejects Wright’s/Talmudic harmonization of mourning vs carpe diem. On 7:3 *kaʿas* is anger/frustration (not “sorrow” with Luther/NIV/NRSV); anger preferred because it matches oppression/death; 7:4 wise = house of mourning, fools = pleasure-denial of death—tensions with carpe diem show Qohelet as confused, not consistently orthodox.

### C-R4-08
- **Locus:** 7:5–7; ~L2683–L2705
- **Quote/anchor:** “wise rebuke… foolish songs… reflects… Proverbs… may be… wake-up call to depressing reality… fool’s laughter… crackle of thorns… under a pot… hebel… much more likely… relative superiority of wisdom over folly… similar… 2:12–16… even a wise person can be made a fool when money becomes involved… Extortion… bribery… Crenshaw… ‘Wisdom does not always succeed; it can be nullified by brute strength or subterfuge.’”

### C-R4-09
- **Locus:** 7:8–10; ~L2707–L2731
- **Quote/anchor:** “end over the beginning… patience over pride… connected with… day of death… day of birth… prohibition against anger… How can Qohelet prefer anger… 7:3 but warn… here?… Whybray… Fox… admirable attempts to harmonize… further evidence of his confusion… Do not say… former days were better… not from wisdom… nothing new under the sun… symptoms of the impatience and pride… v. 8.”
- **Claim:** 7:8: end > beginning (linked to death/birth theme); patience (`'erek ruah`) > pride. 7:9 forbids anger as fool-mark—contradicts 7:3 without textual nuance for dual senses (Whybray/Fox harmonizations rejected). 7:10 forbids nostalgic “former days better”: denies reality of sameness/meaninglessness (1:9 etc.); Whybray/Gordis: nostalgia as impatience/pride of v. 8.

### C-R4-12
- **Locus:** 7:15–22 unit intro; ~L2765–L2767

### C-R4-13
- **Locus:** 7:15; ~L2785–L2797
- **Quote/anchor:** “good people suffering and evil people thriving… tension with… strict idea that one’s actions have a determined and reasonable result… hebel… modifies… ‘days’… temporal translation, ‘brief’… unwarranted… righteous perishing and the wicked living long… cuts across normative biblical expectations… Exod. 20:12; Deut. 4:40… Prov. 3:1–2… Ps. 1… Van Leeuwen… Proverbs as a whole does not teach a simple retribution theology… same conflict… Psalm 73, but without reaching the same resolution.”
- **Claim:** Empirical observation: righteous perish in/through righteousness; wicked live long in evil—paradox vs law/wisdom retribution strands; *hebel* modifies life-days (not “brief”); Van Leeuwen nuance on Proverbs noted, but Qohelet still shocks; Psalm 73 parallel without resolution.

### C-R4-14
- **Locus:** 7:16–17; ~L2799–L2813
- **Quote/anchor:** “not… false pretense… Castellino and Whybray… hithpael of hkm… lack of the hithpael in the first part… syntactical similarity with v. 17… not about those who pretend to be fools… sincere righteousness and true wisdom… Why exert oneself… folly is… totally avoided… leaves open… ‘reasonable’ level of wickedness… far from… Leviticus 19:2… no principle of retribution that assures the righteous that they will be better off.”
- **Claim:** Against pretense reading (Castellino/Whybray): 7:16 warns against real excess righteousness/wisdom (ruin ambiguous: psychological or physical; God or burnout). 7:17: avoid excess wickedness and (unqualified) folly—implies possible “reasonable” wickedness, distant from Lev 19:2 holiness; premature death risk for extremes, not systematic retribution.

- **Quote/anchor:** “seek (bqs), find (ms'), and the sum of things (ḥešbon)… failed… found three things: (1) women were more bitter than death (v. 26); (2) no females and only an occasional male were virtuous (v. 28); (3) though God created all people upright, every single one went wrong… low view of humanity… ḥešbon… explanation that stands behind the world… never achieves… harsh conclusion that everything is ‘meaningless’ (hebel).”

- **Locus:** 9:4–6; ~L3169–L3185

- **Claim:** Life > death only relatively (dog vs lion; ANE contempt for dogs); “hope” is false/consciousness of death. Dead: no knowledge, reward (earthly wages only—not heavenly; Targum/Gregory special pleading), memory, emotions, or portion under the sun.
- **Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R4-35
- **Locus:** 9:7–8; ~L3187–L3197
- **Quote/anchor:** “move from advice to imperative… fifth… carpe diem… not moving from doubt to certainty but rather to urgency in the light of death… God has already approved your deeds… jars… Targum… eschatological… Gregory… mouths of those who hate the Lord… white… joy… not… purity… oil on your head.”
- **Claim:** Stronger carpe diem imperatives (eat/drink; white clothes; oil): urgency from death, not Whybray’s certainty-growth. “God has already approved your deeds” jars—Longman rejects Targum eschatology, Gregory’s “enemies’ speech,” and Ogden’s will-restriction as forced. White = festivity/joy (Brenner), not purity.

### C-R4-36
- **Locus:** 9:9; ~L3199–L3205

- **Claim:** Enjoy life with beloved wife/`iššâ`—Longman prefers marital (Midrash; ancient setting) over promiscuous no-article reading (Jerome/Ibn Ezra/Ginsburg) without changing main point: temporary enjoyment within *hebel* days God gives; reward/portion in toil under the sun.

### C-R4-37
- **Locus:** 9:10; ~L3207–L3213
- **Quote/anchor:** “All that your hand finds to do, do with your power… no action or thought or knowledge or wisdom in the grave… one of the clearest indications that Qohelet had absolutely no concept of life after death… Hengstenberg… special pleading… ‘under the sun’ entails the entirety of human possibility.”
- **Claim:** Seize opportunity now (Judg 9:33; 1 Sam 10:7 idiom)—neither pure license nor mere work-ethic. Sheol ends action, thought, knowledge, wisdom: no afterlife concept in Qohelet; “under the sun” = full human horizon—hence meaning’s elusiveness. Hengstenberg et al. special plead.

### C-R4-38
- **Locus:** 9:11–12; ~L3215–L3241
- **Quote/anchor:** “race is not to the swift… battle not to the mighty… food for the wise… wealth to the clever… favor to the intelligent, but time and chance happen to all… Lauha… Romans 9:16… human inability drives Paul to divine grace, while Qohelet ends up in frustration… no one knows his time… fish… evil net… birds… snare… suddenly… includes the wise.”
- **Claim:** Outcomes not determined by speed, strength, wisdom, cleverness, or intelligence—time and chance rule. Death-time unknown; sudden snare imagery; wise share vulnerability. Contrast: Paul → grace; Qohelet → frustration (Lauha).

### C-R4-39
- **Locus:** 9:13–16; ~L3243–L3269
- **Quote/anchor:** “though wisdom has a short-term effect, it amounts to nothing over the long run… small city… great king… poor but wise man… rescued the city… no one remembered that poor wise man… ‘Wisdom is better than power.’ But the wisdom of the poor man was despised!… Isaksson… ‘might have saved’… less preferred… Targum… allegorical… body… evil spirit… good but humble spirit… short run… long run (see also 4:13–16).”
- **Claim:** Anecdote: poor wise man saves besieged small city but is forgotten; wisdom > power relatively yet despised afterward—short-term benefit, long-term *hebel* (actual rescue preferred to Isaksson’s potential; Targum body/spirit allegory noted as reception).

### C-R4-40

- **Locus:** interlocutors named across range (sample synthesis of attributed debate)
